Furthermore significantly more teachers in the study group asked ‘Why/How’and ‘If/then’questions as opposed to ‘What’ questions asked by the majority of the control group, suggesting that the comparative critique cycle led the study condition teachers to engage in a more detailed and more specific reflection than the vicarious reflection task of the control group.
cells.note: The study text reports a controlled study but does not state that assignment was random; no printed test statistic or effect size is provided.

O.outcome_detail: centering social justice in learning design

cells.quote: We found that attending to social justice requires a reflexive, reflective approach situated within understandings related to designer positionality and power.
cells.note: The study reports a qualitative assertion rather than a measured comparative effect.

D.treatment: design practices that address justice-based tensions

O.outcome_detail: negotiation of tensions around goals, roles, and power

cells.quote: Design practices were employed to address justice-based tensions that emerged around project goals, perceived roles, and power dynamics.
cells.note: The study identifies the practices and tensions qualitatively; it does not report a quantified outcome.

D.treatment: designer attention to positionality and power

cells.quote: Rather than see­ing a designer as an “impersonal technician” tasked with implementing the scientific process of instructional design, scholars argue that both designers and the process of design are situated within historical, social, cultural, and political discourses and ways of knowing (CampBell & Janes, 2021, p. 237).
cells.note: This is a qualitative conceptual contrast informing the cases, not an experimental comparison.

D.comparison: schools with smaller increases in free meal access

result.effect: 1.506 percentage points (p = 0.024); positive but diminishing returns with each additional year of exposure

cells.quote: One study showed that CEP exposure was associated with improved graduation rates at schools with the largest increases in free meal access by 1.506%pt (p = 0.024) [39]. Each additional year of CEP exposure yielded positive but diminishing returns.
cells.note: The study text does not explicitly state the comparison group; the comparison is inferred from the reported contrast between schools with the largest and smaller increases in free meal access.

cells.quote: CEP was associated with a reduction in the likelihood of students being suspended or expelled at least once by 1%pt and strengthened with sustained implementation, with a reduction of 1.6%pt by the third year post-implementation [36].
cells.note: The review synthesizes nonrandomized difference-in-differences studies; the comparison is the non-CEP condition implied by the reported CEP association.

cells.quote: Similarly, a 2024 study found that CEP was associated with a lower probability of suspension for middle school students by nearly 2%pt [35]
cells.note: The study text reports a nonrandomized association summarized in the review; the comparison is the non-CEP condition implied by the reported CEP association.

cells.quote: For high school students, CEP reduced the probability of suspension by nearly 2.5%pt [35]
cells.note: The study text reports a nonrandomized association summarized in the review; the comparison is the non-CEP condition implied by the reported CEP association.

cells.quote: A 2021 study found that attending a CEP school increased the probability of daily school attendance by 0.24 percentage points [%pt] (p < 0.01) [30].
cells.note: The review reports a national difference-in-differences study of CEP and attendance.

O.outcome_detail: standardized reading and math test scores

cells.quote: Both studies showed that CEP did not improve academic performance in test scores [30, 37].
cells.note: The text reports no overall test-score improvement; no equivalence test or adequate-power claim is given, so the result is coded ns rather than 0.

result.effect: more than twice as likely to attend school

cells.quote: Another study assessed a districtwide BATB program and found that participants were more than twice as likely to attend school as non‐participants [34].
cells.note: The review synthesizes naturalistic school-policy studies and reports the new districtwide BATB finding.

result.effect: null in adjusted models; unadjusted reading improvements

cells.quote: Although unadjusted models showed improvements in reading scores following program participation, adjusted models found no significant changes in reading or math scores over time [34].
cells.note: BATB academic-achievement findings were mixed across models and across the broader prior review.

O.outcome_detail: Standardized reading and math test scores

cells.quote: Two studies focused on the association between standardized test scores and CEP. Both studies showed that CEP did not improve academic performance in test scores [30, 37].
cells.note: Synthesis of two studies; the text does not report an equivalence test or adequate power.

D.treatment: CEP exposure in districts with baseline low free meal eligibility

O.outcome_detail: Math performance, particularly among Hispanic students

cells.quote: A 2022 study showed that overall, CEP did not improve overall reading or math performance, but improvements in math were observed among the subsample for which CEP led to the largest increases in free meal access (i.e., baseline low free meal eligibility), particularly among Hispanic students [37].
cells.note: Subgroup finding from Ruffini; the printed effect size is not provided in the study text above.

cells.quote: "We judged the certainty of the evidence to be moderate for 16 teaching strategies, low to moderate for one, low for 11, and very low for 10 ( Table 7). We did not judge the certainty of the evidence to by high for any of the teaching strategies."
cells.note: The supplied study text does not report the treatment-versus-comparison direction or printed effect sizes for the 37 strategies; this quote is from the wiki entry, not the study text.
